title: Artificial intelligence and continuous renal replacement therapy

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Artificial intelligence and continuous renal replacement therapy》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · S0001-p1】Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is an extracorporeal support technique that mimics renal function, primarily used for treating severe acute kidney injury (AKI), especially for patients with hemodynamic instability [1]. Through continuous blood purification employing various techniques with distinct solute clearance modalities, CRRT can effectively maintain patients’ internal homeostasis and reduce the burden on the kidneys. With the continuous development of technology, the application of CRRT has been expanded to support multiple organs, including cardiac, hepatic, and pulmonary functions, and can provide vital life support for patients with multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) [2]. However, CRRT is not a fixed intervention. Treatment initiation, modality selection, delivered dose, anticoagulation, net ultrafiltration, electrolyte management, filter performance, and liberation from therapy require repeated reassessment as the patient’s condition changes. This complexity poses substantial challenges to individualized treatment, efficient use of clinical resources, and consistent delivery of high-quality CRRT.

【Introduction · S0001-p2】CRRT still faces several unresolved challenges in clinical practice. CRRT data come from multiple sources, such as electronic health records (EHRs), bedside monitors, laboratory systems, nursing records, and CRRT devices, and are often collected at different times and in different formats. Clinicians therefore need to interpret large amounts of heterogeneous and time-dependent information while managing common complications, including hemodynamic instability, circuit clotting or filter failure, electrolyte disturbances, and unplanned treatment interruptions [3–5]. CRRT initiation, treatment adjustment, and discontinuation remain difficult because patient characteristics and treatment responses vary across different patient groups and clinical settings. In addition, frequent alarms, limited clinical resources, and unequal access to nephrology expertise may further affect the consistency and quality of CRRT care.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Artificial intelligence and continuous renal replacement therapy》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Methods · S0002-p1】This narrative review was informed by a structured literature search to summarize the current evidence and potential applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). From inception to July 22, 2026, we searched three electronic databases, including PubMed, Embase, and Scopus. The search strategy included two main concepts: CRRT-related terms and AI-related terms. The former included “continuous renal replacement therapy,” “continuous kidney replacement therapy,” “CKRT,” “CRRT,” “CVVH,” “CVVHD,” and “CVVHDF.” The latter included “algorithm,” “artificial intelligence,” “chatbot,” “ChatGPT,” “clinical decision support,” “data-driven,” “deep learning,” “foundation model,” “generative AI,” “generative artificial intelligence,” “gradient boost,” “language model,” “large language model,” “long short-term memory,” “LSTM,” “machine learning,” “natural language processing,” “neural network,” “predictive model,” “random forest,” “reinforcement learning,” “support vector machine,” “transfer learning,” and “XGBoost.” Preprints, grey literature, and conference abstracts or reports lacking sufficient methodological details were excluded according to predefined eligibility criteria.

【AI framework and task-method matching in CRRT · S0003-p2】Machine learning encompasses several learning paradigms, including supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning [16]. Among these, supervised learning uses labeled input-output pairs to learn a predictive mapping from input features to target outcomes [17,18], holding significant potential especially for clinical data [19], such as laboratory tests, vital signs, and medications. The clinical data are usually recorded in predetermined formats and fields, with values commonly represented as numerical measurements or discrete categorical entries. In CRRT research, supervised prediction models have been developed in specific patient populations to predict CRRT requirement, survival or mortality, hypotension, circuit clotting, successful discontinuation, and renal function recovery [7,8,10,11,20–22].

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Artificial intelligence and continuous renal replacement therapy》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Validation, governance, and clinical value · S0005-S2003-p1】Good model performance alone is not enough for clinical implementation. Before clinical use, model performance should be evaluated using data that were not used for model development and that represent the intended patient population [38,39]. Evaluation should include discrimination, calibration, clinical utility, and performance in important patient subgroups [38,39]. Models with acceptable performance should then be evaluated prospectively to determine their safety, effects on clinical decisions, and effects on patient outcomes. Popoff et al. proposed a similar staged approach for their CRRT-weaning model, with prospective evaluation followed by randomized testing if the initial results were favorable [48].

【Validation, governance, and clinical value · S0005-S2003-p2】Clinical implementation also requires attention to data security, patient privacy, bias, and responsibility for AI-assisted decisions [63]. Clinical AI is increasingly shaped by international and national frameworks, including guidance from the World Health Organization, China’s guidance for AI medical devices, the European Union AI Act, and Good Machine Learning Practice principles [66–69]. Nephrology-specific ethical guidance has also emerged [70], while a dedicated regulatory framework for AI in CRRT has not yet been established. Cost, staff training, and integration with existing clinical systems should also be considered [63]. Although some studies suggest that AI-supported anemia management may be cost-effective in hemodialysis patients [71,72], economic evidence specific to CRRT remains lacking. Model performance and fairness should continue to be assessed after implementation [39]. In CRRT, a practical approach would be to move from retrospective model development and evaluation in independent data to prospective clinical evaluation, followed by clinician-supervised use and continued assessment of clinical impact, cost, and model performance. Implementation should be adapted to institutional readiness, considering factors such as data availability, digital infrastructure, workflow integration, and capacity for AI model evaluation [73]. Centers with limited resources may begin with validated tools using routinely available clinical data, centers with moderate resources may add local prospective validation and workflow integration, and centers with advanced resources may progress to real-time device integration and locally adapted models.
